subject: history
displayName: KS3 History — Tudor Monarchs & the Reformation
subtitle: Henry VIII's break with Rome, the English Reformation, and the reigns of Edward VI and Mary I.

data.targetWord: The ruling family of England from Henry VII in 1485 to Elizabeth I in 1603.

examples.en-GB: The Tudor dynasty began when Henry VII won the Battle of Bosworth in 1485.

data.targetWord: The belief that a ruler has a lawful and accepted right to rule.

examples.en-GB: Henry VII had to work hard to establish his legitimacy after winning at Bosworth.

data.targetWord: The order in which power passes from one ruler to the next.

examples.en-GB: Succession was a major concern for Henry VIII, who wanted a male heir.

data.targetWord: A religious movement that challenged Catholic beliefs and the authority of the Pope, leading to the growth of Protestant churches.

examples.en-GB: The Reformation changed the religious landscape of England under the Tudor monarchs.

data.targetWord: The principle that the monarch, not the Pope, is the highest authority over the Church in England.

examples.en-GB: Henry VIII established royal supremacy through the Act of Supremacy in 1534.

data.targetWord: A law passed in 1534 that recognised Henry VIII as Supreme Head of the Church of England.

examples.en-GB: The Act of Supremacy made Henry VIII, not the Pope, the head of the Church of England.

data.targetWord: A legal decision that a marriage was never valid in the first place.

examples.en-GB: Henry VIII sought an annulment from Catherine of Aragon to marry Anne Boleyn.

data.targetWord: The closing down of monasteries by Henry VIII between 1536 and 1540, transferring their wealth to the Crown.

examples.en-GB: The dissolution of the monasteries changed the religious and economic landscape of England.

data.targetWord: A religious community where monks or nuns lived, prayed, worked, and often provided charity to local communities.

examples.en-GB: The monks in the monastery provided food and shelter for the poor in the surrounding area.

data.targetWord: Religious belief judged by the authorities to be dangerously false, often punishable by death.

examples.en-GB: Under Mary I, hundreds of Protestants were burned for heresy.

data.targetWord: Information, images, or messages designed to shape what people think about a ruler or government.

examples.en-GB: Tudor monarchs used propaganda in portraits and proclamations to present themselves as powerful.

data.targetWord: A large rebellion in northern England in 1536 protesting against Henry VIII's religious changes and monastery closures.

examples.en-GB: The Pilgrimage of Grace showed widespread opposition to Henry VIII's religious reforms.

data.targetWord: A Protestant prayer book introduced under Edward VI that established English-language church services.

examples.en-GB: The introduction of the Book of Common Prayer under Edward VI caused protests in some areas.

data.targetWord: A Christian who follows churches that developed from the Reformation and rejects the authority of the Pope.

examples.en-GB: Edward VI's advisers promoted Protestant reforms in England's churches.

data.targetWord: A Christian who accepts the authority of the Pope and follows the traditions of the Roman Catholic Church.

examples.en-GB: Mary I was Catholic and restored links with Rome after the Protestant reforms of Edward VI.

data.targetWord: A family of rulers who pass power from one generation to another.

examples.en-GB: The Tudor dynasty ruled England for over a century, from 1485 to 1603.

data.targetWord: Henry VIII's chief minister who organised the break with Rome and supervised the dissolution of the monasteries.

examples.en-GB: Thomas Cromwell sent commissioners to investigate monasteries before their closure.

data.targetWord: The name given to Henry VIII's attempt to end his marriage to Catherine of Aragon and obtain an annulment from the Pope.

examples.en-GB: The Great Matter led to a political and religious crisis when the Pope refused to grant Henry VIII an annulment.

data.targetWord: A queen who rules in her own right, not merely as the wife of a king.

examples.en-GB: Mary I was England's first queen regnant, ruling independently in her own right.

data.targetWord: The Parliament that met from 1529 to 1536 and passed laws reducing the Pope's authority and increasing the king's control over the Church.

examples.en-GB: The Reformation Parliament passed the Act of Supremacy that made Henry VIII head of the Church.

data.targetWord: A series of civil wars between the Houses of Lancaster and York for control of the English throne, which ended at the Battle of Bosworth in 1485.

examples.en-GB: Henry VII's victory in the Wars of the Roses established the Tudor dynasty.

data.targetWord: The head of the Roman Catholic Church, based in Rome, whose authority Henry VIII rejected in 1534.

examples.en-GB: The Pope refused to grant Henry VIII's request for an annulment from Catherine of Aragon.

data.targetWord: A strict Protestant who wanted to remove more Catholic-style practices from the Church of England and simplify worship.

examples.en-GB: Puritans criticised Elizabeth I's Religious Settlement for keeping too many Catholic traditions.

data.targetWord: An official public announcement made by the monarch or government to inform subjects of laws or expectations.

examples.en-GB: Henry VIII used proclamations to inform his subjects of religious changes.

data.targetWord: Archbishop of Canterbury who supported Protestant reform and helped shape English Protestant worship under Henry VIII and Edward VI.

examples.en-GB: Thomas Cranmer compiled the Book of Common Prayer used in Edward VI's Protestant churches.

data.targetWord: A 1559 agreement that made England officially Protestant while keeping some traditional features in church worship and appearance.

examples.en-GB: The Elizabethan Religious Settlement tried to create a broad Church that both moderate Catholics and Protestants could accept.

The ____ of Grace in 1536 was a major rebellion in northern England against Henry VIII's religious changes.
Edward VI became king at the age of ____ when Henry VIII died in 1547.
The first Book of ____ Prayer was introduced in 1549 during Edward VI's reign.
Mary I married ____ of Spain in 1554, worrying many English people about foreign influence.
Between 1555 and 1558, around ____ Protestants were burned for heresy under Mary I.
Thomas More was executed in 1535 for refusing to accept Henry VIII's ____.
Henry VII married Elizabeth of York to unite the houses of ____ and York.
Elizabeth I became queen in ____ after the death of Mary I.
Elizabeth I used the title 'Supreme ____' of the Church of England, not Supreme Head.
Martin Luther challenged Catholic practices in Europe in ____, helping start the Reformation.
Henry VIII's chief minister ____ Wolsey failed to secure an annulment from the Pope.
Lady Jane Grey ruled as queen for only ____ days before Mary I took the throne.
Henry VIII's break with Rome was a change in ____, not an instant Protestant revolution.

The ____ rose symbol combined red Lancaster and white York to show Tudor unity.

data.title: Put the Tudor monarchs in the correct order of reign
Order the key events of Henry VIII's break with Rome
items: Henry VIII tries to end his marriage to Catherine of Aragon (1527)
Reformation Parliament begins reducing papal authority (1529)
Act of Supremacy makes Henry Supreme Head of the Church (1534)

data.title: Order the religious changes across the Tudor period
items: Henry VIII breaks with Rome but keeps many Catholic beliefs (1534)
Edward VI introduces Protestant reforms and the Book of Common Prayer (1549)
Mary I restores Catholicism and links with Rome (1553)
Elizabeth I creates a Protestant settlement with some compromise (1559)

data.title: Sort the causes of Henry VIII's break with Rome

pairs.text: Henry wanted to marry Anne Boleyn
Henry needed a male heir for the Tudor dynasty
Henry wanted to control the Church in England
Parliament was used to pass religious laws
Church lands and wealth could strengthen the Crown
The dissolution of the monasteries raised money
Martin Luther challenged the Pope's authority in Europe
